facts.statement: Orthacanthus lived during the Upper Carboniferous to the Lower Permian periods.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Upper Carboniferous - Lower Permian

facts.statement: The genus Orthacanthus was named by Louis Agassiz in 1843.
facts.quote: authority: Agassiz, 1843

facts.statement: Orthacanthus is an extinct genus of freshwater cartilaginous fish in the order Xenacanthiformes.
facts.quote: Orthacanthus is an extinct genus of fresh-water xenacanthiform cartilaginous fish, named by Louis Agassiz in 1843

facts.statement: Orthacanthus lived a nektobenthic lifestyle and had a carnivorous diet.
facts.quote: Orthacanthus had a nektobenthic life habitat, with a carnivorous diet

facts.statement: Evidence suggests that adult Orthacanthus practiced filial cannibalism by preying on juveniles of their own species.
facts.quote: Multiple authors have also discovered evidence of cannibalism in the diet of Orthacanthus and of "filial cannibalism" where adult Orthacanthus preyed upon juvenile Orthacanthus

facts.statement: In the Late Carboniferous and Early Permian, Orthacanthus was an apex predator in freshwater swamps and bayous across Europe and North America.
facts.quote: During the Late Carboniferous-Early Permian, Orthacanthus was an apex predator of freshwater swamps and bayous in Europe and North America

facts.statement: Mature individuals of Orthacanthus could reach a length of nearly 3 meters (10 feet).
facts.quote: Mature Orthacanthus reached nearly 3 meters (10 feet) in length

facts.statement: Orthacanthus teeth possess at least three cusps, including two principal serrated cusps and an intermediate cusp.
facts.quote: Orthacanthus teeth have a minimum of three cusps, two principal cusps, and an intermediate cusp, where the principal cusps are variously serrated

facts.statement: Louis Agassiz erected the genera Orthacanthus and Pleuracanthus based on isolated ichthyodorulites found in the British Carboniferous System.
facts.quote: The two genera Orthacanthus and Pleuracanthus were erected by Louis Agassiz based on isolated "ichthyodorulites" from the British Carboniferous System

facts.statement: The initial fossils of Orthacanthus were found in the United Kingdom at locations including Dudley, Leeds, North Wales, Carluke, and Edinburgh.
facts.quote: They were initially found in the United Kingdom in Dudley, Leeds, North Wales, Carluke, and Edinburgh

facts.statement: A well-preserved impression of Orthacanthus from Ruppelsdorf, Bohemia, was described by Goldfuss.
facts.quote: A well preserved impression from Ruppelsdorf, Bohemia, was described by Goldfuss

facts.statement: The larger teeth of Orthacanthus compressus are distinguished from those of O. texensis by a more pronounced basal tubercle.
facts.quote: The larger teeth of Orthacanthus compressus and Orthacanthus texensis are differentiated by a more pronounced basal tubercle in O. compressus

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the size difference between large and small adult teeth in O. compressus might indicate sexual dimorphism.
facts.quote: The difference in characteristics between the large and small O. compressus adult teeth might indicate sexual dimorphism

facts.statement: Analysis of O. platypternus spines indicates sexual dimorphism, with females possessing larger spines than males in subadult and young adult stages.
facts.quote: The spines of O. platypternus showing 3 to 4 dentine layers are interpreted to be subadults or young adults, and are separated into two size classes where females have the largest spines in comparison to males, indicating sexual dimorphism

facts.statement: Dorsal spines of O. platypternus from Texas preserve a highly vascularized wall composed mainly of centrifugally growing dentine.
facts.quote: The dorsal spines of Orthacanthus platypternus from the Craddock Bone Bed in Texas, USA, preserve a highly vascularized wall mainly composed of centrifugally growing dentine

facts.statement: The periodic deposition of dentine layers in O. platypternus spines likely corresponds to seasonal changes in water temperature and food availability.
facts.quote: These dentine layers are likely deposited periodically in accordance with seasonal variations in water temperature and food availability

facts.statement: The Orthacanthus spine grows from a deep dermal position forming trabecular dentine to a superficial location forming lamellar dentine.
facts.quote: The spine is superficially inserted in the skin, where it grows and moves from a deep position in the dermis where trabecular dentine forms, to a superficial location where centrifugally growing lamellar dentine forms

facts.statement: Orthacanthus is classified within the order Xenacanthiformes, a group of shark-like cartilaginous fish.
facts.quote: Orthacanthus is placed within the broader order Xenacanthiformes, along with a number of other similar shark-like cartilaginous fish

facts.statement: There is an ongoing scientific debate regarding whether Orthacanthus had an obligate freshwater lifestyle or a euryhaline diadromous one.
facts.quote: thus contributing to the controversy between an obligate freshwater or euryhaline diadromous lifestyle

facts.statement: Isotopic analysis suggests that O. buxieri inhabited freshwater lakes.
facts.quote: Paired bioapatite δ18O, δ13C, and δ34S analysis of O. buxieri suggested that the species was an inhabitant of freshwater lakes

facts.statement: Fossil evidence from the Upper Carboniferous in Spain shows that Orthacanthus preyed on Triodus.
facts.quote: Cranial remains of specimens of both Orthacanthus and Triodus from the Upper Carboniferous in Puertollano basin, Spain, give evidence of this predator-prey relationship.

facts.statement: Triodus spines found inside the mouth cavity of Orthacanthus fossils provide direct evidence of predation.
facts.quote: Numerous and well preserved cephalic elements of Triodus were associated with the cranial remains of Orthacanthus, and is explained by the inclusion of occipital spines of Triodus in the buccal cavity of Orthacanthus.

facts.statement: Analysis of fossilized feces suggests Orthacanthus engaged in cannibalism by eating juveniles when food was scarce.
facts.quote: Examination of Orthacanthus coprolites from Canada by Aodhan O' Gogain et al. revealed that in times of hardship, Orthacanthus was likely cannibalistic, as teeth from juvenile Orthacanthus were found within the coprolites of adults.

facts.statement: Orthacanthus produced spiral-shaped feces because of its corkscrew-shaped rectum.
facts.quote: The feces of Orthacanthus has a spiral shape due to a corkscrew-shaped rectum.

facts.statement: The oldest known Orthacanthus fossil dates to the Lower Devonian, approximately 407 to 393 million years ago.
facts.quote: The oldest known specimen of Orthacanthus, Diplodus problematicus, was found in New Brunswick, Canada, in the Lower Devonian (Emsian, c. 407 to 393 million years ago).

facts.statement: Orthacanthus fossils have been discovered in the US, UK, Poland, and France.
facts.quote: Other specimens have been found in locations including the US, the United Kingdom, Poland, and France.

facts.statement: The genus Orthacanthus was named by Agassiz in 1843.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Agassiz, 1843

facts.statement: Orthacanthus lived in marine environments with a nectobenthic habitat and a carnivorous diet.
facts.quote: Orthacanthus vivía en ambientes marinos y tenía un hábitat de vida nectobentónico, con una dieta carnívora.

facts.statement: About 260 million years ago, Orthacanthus was a top predator in freshwater swamps and bayous across Europe and North America.
facts.quote: Hace unos 260 millones de años, Orthacanthus fue un superpredador de pantanos de agua dulce y bayous en Europa y América del Norte.

facts.statement: Adult Orthacanthus reached a length of nearly 3 meters.
facts.quote: Los Orthacanthus adultos alcanzaron casi 3 metros de longitud.

facts.statement: Orthacanthus teeth had at least three cusps, with complex base morphology and diverse serration on the main cusps.
facts.quote: Los dientes de Orthacanthus tienen un mínimo de tres cúspides, dos cúspides principales y una cúspide intermedia, donde las cúspides principales son dentadas de forma diversa, con una morfología de base compleja.

facts.statement: Juvenile Orthacanthus compressus teeth were longer than wide, had thin bases, and lacked serrations.
facts.quote: Los dientes juveniles de O. compressus son más largos que anchos, tienen una base más delgada y carecen de sierras, similares a los dientes de O. platypternus.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Craddock Bonebed in Texas show evidence of bone resorption and enamel pearls in Orthacanthus platypternus.
facts.quote: Orthacanthus platypternus de la capa Craddock Bonebed en Texas, EE. UU., muestra evidencia de resorción ósea y el equivalente de una "perla esmaltada".

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that size differences between large and small adult teeth of O. compressus might indicate sexual dimorphism.
facts.quote: La diferencia de características entre los dientes adultos grandes y pequeños de O. compressus podría indicar dimorfismo sexual.

facts.statement: The genus Orthacanthus contains three species: O. arcuatus, O. cylindricus, and O. senckenbergianus.
facts.quote: El género contiene tres especies: Orthacanthus arcuatus Newberry, 1856 Orthacanthus cylindricus Agassiz, 1843 Orthacanthus senckenbergianus

facts.statement: The type species for the genus Orthacanthus is Pleuracanthus cylindricus.
facts.quote: Type species: Pleuracanthus cylindricus

facts.statement: The genus Orthacanthus lived from the Emsian to the Kimmeridgian, spanning 410.62 to 149.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Emsian to Kimmeridgian (410.62 to 149.2 million years ago)
